content: 1. Serious and potentially fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylactoid reactions, have been reported in patients receiving penicillin therapy. These reactions are more common with parenteral administration but can also occur with oral penicillins. 2. Individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens are at a higher risk of experiencing these reactions. 3. Severe hypersensitivity reactions have been documented in patients with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity when treated with cephalosporins. 4. Before initiating penicillin therapy, a thorough inquiry into the patient’s history of hypersensitivity to penicillins, cephalosporins, and other allergens should be conducted. 5. If an allergic reaction occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. 6. Severe anaphylactoid reactions require emergency treatment, including epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous steroids, and airway management, such as intubation, as clinically indicated. 7. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including injectable ampicillin. The severity can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. 8. Antibacterial therapy disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. 9. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. 10. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even if it occurs up to two months after the last dose. 11. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be implemented as clinically indicated. 12. During therapy, the possibility of superinfections with fungal organisms or bacterial pathogens should be considered. If superinfection occurs, the drug should be discontinued, and appropriate treatment should be initiated. 13. A high percentage (43–100%) of patients with infectious mononucleosis who receive ampicillin develop a skin rash. The rash typically appears 7–10 days after starting oral ampicillin therapy and resolves within a few days to a week after discontinuation of the drug. 14. The rash is usually maculopapular, pruritic, and generalized. Therefore, ampicillin is not recommended for patients with mononucleosis. It is unclear whether these patients are truly allergic to ampicillin. 15. Prescribing ampicillin in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 16. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including ampicillin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). 17. When prescribed for bacterial infections, patients should be advised to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. 18. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance, making them untreatable with ampicillin or other antibacterial drugs in the future. 19. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, watery and bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, may occur even two or more months after the last dose of the antibiotic. If this occurs, patients should contact their physician immediately. 20. Periodic assessment of organ system function, including renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic systems, should be performed during prolonged therapy with ampicillin. 21. Transient elevation of serum transaminases has been observed following ampicillin administration, but the clinical significance of this finding is unknown. 22. Concurrent administration of allopurinol and ampicillin significantly increases the incidence of skin rashes compared to patients receiving ampicillin alone. It is unclear whether this is due to allopurinol or the hyperuricemia present in these patients. 23. High urine concentrations of ampicillin may cause false-positive glucose reactions if Clinitest, Benedict’s Solution, or Fehling’s Solution are used. Glucose tests based on enzymatic glucose oxidase reactions (e.g., Clinistix or Tes-Tape) are recommended. 24. No long-term animal studies have been conducted with ampicillin. 25. Reproduction studies in laboratory animals at doses several times the human dose have shown no evidence of adverse effects due to ampicillin. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. 26. Because animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, ampicillin should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. 27. Oral ampicillin-class antibiotics are poorly absorbed during labor. 28. Studies in guinea pigs have shown that intravenous administration of ampicillin slightly decreases uterine tone and contraction frequency but moderately increases the height and duration of contractions. 29. It is unknown whether the use of ampicillin in humans during labor or delivery has immediate or delayed adverse effects on the fetus, prolongs labor, or increases the likelihood of obstetrical interventions or neonatal resuscitation. 30. Ampicillin is excreted in trace amounts in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administering ampicillin-class antibiotics to nursing women. 31. Guidelines for administering ampicillin to children are provided in the Dosage and Administration section.
